Etymology and nomenclature
Centauri (Latinised to Alpha Centauri) is the system's designation given by J. Bayer in 1603. It belongs to the
constellation <color=#3366CC>Centaurus</color>, named after the <color=#3366CC>part human, part horse creature</color> in Greek mythology; <color=#3366CC>Heracles</color> accidentally
wounded the centaur and placed him in the sky after his death. Alpha Centauri marks the right front hoof of the
Centaur. The common name Rigil Kentaurus is a Latinisation of the Arabic translation Rijl al-Qintūrus, meaning "the
Foot of the Centaur". Qintūrus is the Arabic transliteration of the Greek (Kentaurus). The name is frequently
abbreviated to Rigil Kent or even Rigil, though the latter name is better known for <color=#3366CC>Rigel</color> ( Orionis).
An alternative name found in European sources, Toliman, is an approximation of the Arabic az-Zalīmān (in older
transcription, at-Thalīmān), meaning 'the (two male) Ostriches', an appellation Zakariya al-Qazwini had applied to the
pair of stars Lambda and Mu Sagittarii; it was often unclear on old star maps which name was intended to go with
which star (or stars), and the referents changed over time. The name Toliman originates with Jacob Golius' 1669
edition of Al-Farghani's Compendium. Tolimân is Golius' Latinisation of the Arabic name al-Zulmān "the ostriches", the
name of an asterism of which Alpha Centauri formed the main star.
Centauri C was discovered in 1915 by Robert T. A. Innes, who suggested that it be named Proxima Centaurus,. The
name Proxima Centauri later became more widely used and is now listed by the <color=#3366CC>International Astronomical Union</color> (IAU)
as the approved proper name; it is frequently abbreviated to Proxima.
In 2016, the Working Group on Star Names of the IAU, having decided to attribute proper names to individual
component stars rather than to <color=#3366CC>multiple systems</color>, approved the name Rigil Kentaurus as being restricted to Centauri A
and the name Proxima Centauri for Centauri C. On 10 August 2018, the <color=#3366CC>IAU</color> approved the name Toliman for Centauri
B.
Other names
During the 19th century, the northern amateur popularist E.H. Burritt used the now-obscure name Bungula. Although its
origin is not known, it may have been coined from the Greek letter beta and Latin ungula 'hoof', originally for <color=#3366CC>Beta</color>
<color=#3366CC>Centauri</color> (the other hoof).
In Chinese astronomy, Nán Mén, meaning Southern Gate, refers to an <color=#3366CC>asterism</color> consisting of Alpha Centauri and
Epsilon Centauri. Consequently, the <color=#3366CC>Chinese name</color> for Alpha Centauri itself is Nán Mén Èr, the Second Star of the
Southern Gate.
To the Indigenous Boorong clan of the Wergaia people of northwestern <color=#3366CC>Victoria</color> in Australia, Alpha Centauri and <color=#3366CC>Beta</color>
<color=#3366CC>Centauri</color> are Bermbermgle, two brothers noted for their courage and destructiveness, who speared and killed Tchingal
'The Emu' (the <color=#3366CC>Coalsack Nebula</color>). The form in Wotjobaluk is Bram-bram-bult.
The Mursi people of Ethiopia call this star Sholbi; it forms an <color=#3366CC>asterism</color> with Crucis (Imai), <color=#3366CC>Crucis</color> (Thaadoi), and <color=#3366CC>Centauri</color>
(Waar).
Observation
To the naked eye, Centauri AB appear to be a single star, the brightest in the southern constellation of Centaurus.
Their apparent angular separation varies over about 80 years between 2 and 22 <color=#3366CC>arcseconds</color> (the naked eye has a
resolution of 60 arcsec), but through much of the orbit, both are easily resolved in binoculars or small telescopes. At
0.27 <color=#3366CC>apparent magnitude</color> (combined for A and B magnitudes ), Alpha Centauri is a first-magnitude star and is fainter
only than <color=#3366CC>Sirius</color> and <color=#3366CC>Canopus</color>. It is the outer star of The Pointers or The Southern Pointers, so called because the line
through <color=#3366CC>Beta Centauri</color> (Hadar/Agena), some 4.5° west, points to the constellation <color=#3366CC>Crux</color>—the Southern Cross. The
Pointers easily distinguish the true Southern Cross from the fainter <color=#3366CC>asterism</color> known as the <color=#3366CC>False Cross</color>.
South of about 29° South latitude, Cen is circumpolar and never sets below the horizon. North of about 29° N latitude,
Alpha Centauri never rises. Alpha Centauri lies close to the southern horizon when viewed from latitude 29° N to the

<color=#3366CC>equator</color> (close to <color=#3366CC>Hermosillo</color> and <color=#3366CC>Chihuahua City</color> in <color=#3366CC>Mexico</color>; Galveston, Texas; Ocala, Florida; and <color=#3366CC>Lanzarote</color>, the
<color=#3366CC>Canary Islands</color> of <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>), but only for a short time around its culmination. The star culminates each year at local
midnight on 24 April and at local 9 p.m. on 8 June.
As seen from Earth, Proxima Centauri is 2.2° southwest from Centauri AB; this distance is about four times the <color=#3366CC>angular</color>
<color=#3366CC>diameter</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Moon</color>. Proxima Centauri appears as a deep-red star of a typical apparent magnitude of 11.1 in a
sparsely populated star field, requiring moderately sized telescopes to be seen. Listed as V645 Cen in the General
Catalogue of Variable Stars, version 4.2, this <color=#3366CC>UV Ceti star</color> or "flare star" can unexpectedly brighten rapidly by as much
as 0.6 <color=#3366CC>magnitude</color> at visual wavelengths, then fade after only a few minutes. Some amateur and professional
astronomers regularly monitor for outbursts using either optical or radio telescopes. In August 2015, the largest
recorded flares of the star occurred, with the star becoming 8.3 times brighter than normal on 13 August, in the <color=#3366CC>B band</color>
<color=#3366CC>(blue light region)</color>.
Observational history
Alpha Centauri is listed in the 2nd century star catalog appended to <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Almagest</color>. Ptolemy gave its ecliptic
coordinates, but texts differ as to whether the ecliptic latitude reads 44° 10′ south or 41° 10′ south (presently the ecliptic
latitude is 43.5° south, but it has decreased by a fraction of a degree since <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color>'s time due to <color=#3366CC>proper motion</color>). In
Ptolemy's time, Alpha Centauri was visible from <color=#3366CC>Alexandria, Egypt</color>, at 31° N, but, due to <color=#3366CC>precession</color>, its declination is
now –60° 51′ South, and it can no longer be seen at that latitude. English explorer Robert Hues brought Alpha Centauri
to the attention of European observers in his 1592 work Tractatus de Globis, along with Canopus and <color=#3366CC>Achernar</color>, noting:
Now, therefore, there are but three Stars of the first magnitude that I could perceive in all those parts which are never
seene here in <color=#3366CC>England</color>. The first of these is that bright Star in the sterne of <color=#3366CC>Argo</color> which they call Canobus [Canopus].
The second [Achernar] is in the end of <color=#3366CC>Eridanus</color>. The third [Alpha Centauri] is in the right foote of the <color=#3366CC>Centaure</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>binary</color> nature of Alpha Centauri AB was recognized in December 1689 by Jean Richaud, while observing a
passing <color=#3366CC>comet</color> from his station in Puducherry. Alpha Centauri was only the third binary star to be discovered, preceded
by Mizar AB and <color=#3366CC>Acrux</color>.
The large proper motion of Alpha Centauri AB was discovered by Manuel John Johnson, observing from <color=#3366CC>Saint Helena</color>,
who informed Thomas Henderson at the Royal Observatory, Cape of Good Hope of it. The parallax of Alpha Centauri
was subsequently determined by Henderson from many exacting positional observations of the AB system between
April 1832 and May 1833. He withheld his results, however, because he suspected they were too large to be true, but
eventually published them in 1839 after <color=#3366CC>Bessel</color> released his own accurately determined parallax for 61 Cygni in 1838.
For this reason, Alpha Centauri is sometimes considered as the second star to have its distance measured because
Henderson's work was not fully acknowledged at first. (The distance of Alpha Centauri from the Earth is now reckoned
at 4.396 <color=#3366CC>light-years</color> or 4.396 ly.)
<color=#3366CC>John Herschel</color> made the first micrometrical observations in 1834. Since the early 20th century, measures have been
made with <color=#3366CC>photographic plates</color>.
By 1926, William Stephen Finsen calculated the approximate <color=#3366CC>orbit elements</color> close to those now accepted for this
system. All future positions are now sufficiently accurate for visual observers to determine the relative places of the
stars from a binary star <color=#3366CC>ephemeris</color>. Others, like D. Pourbaix (2002), have regularly refined the precision of new
published orbital elements.
Robert T. A. Innes discovered <color=#3366CC>Proxima Centauri</color> in 1915 by blinking photographic plates taken at different times during
a <color=#3366CC>proper motion</color> survey. These showed large proper motion and parallax similar in both size and direction to those of
Centauri AB, which suggested that Proxima Centauri is part of the Centauri system and slightly closer to <color=#3366CC>Earth</color> than
Centauri AB. As a result, Innes concluded that Proxima Centauri was the closest star to Earth yet discovered.
Location and motion
Alpha Centauri may be inside the <color=#3366CC>G-cloud</color> of the <color=#3366CC>Local Bubble</color>, and its nearest known system is the binary <color=#3366CC>brown dwarf</color>
system Luhman 16, at 3.6 ly distance.
Historical distance estimates
Kinematics
All components of Centauri display significant <color=#3366CC>proper motion</color> against the background sky. Over centuries, this causes
their apparent positions to slowly change. Proper motion was unknown to ancient astronomers. Most assumed that the
stars were permanently fixed on the <color=#3366CC>celestial sphere</color>, as stated in the works of the philosopher Aristotle. In 1718,
<color=#3366CC>Edmond Halley</color> found that some stars had significantly moved from their ancient <color=#3366CC>astrometric</color> positions.
In the 1830s, Thomas Henderson discovered the true distance to Centauri by analysing his many astrometric mural
circle observations. He then realised this system also likely had a high proper motion. In this case, the apparent stellar
motion was found using Nicolas Louis de Lacaille's astrometric observations of 1751–1752, by the observed
differences between the two measured positions in different epochs.
Calculated proper motion of the centre of mass for Centauri AB is about 3620 mas/y (milliarcseconds per year) toward
the west and 694 mas/y toward the north, giving an overall motion of 3686 mas/y in a direction 11° north of west. The
motion of the centre of mass is about 6.1 <color=#3366CC>arcmin</color> each century, or 1.02<color=#3366CC>°</color> each millennium. The speed in the western
direction is 23.0 km/s and in the northerly direction 4.4 km/s. Using <color=#3366CC>spectroscopy</color> the mean radial velocity has been
determined to be around 22.4 km/s towards the Solar System. This gives a speed with respect to the Sun of 32.4 km/s,
very close to the peak in the distribution of speeds of nearby stars.
Since Centauri AB is almost exactly in the plane of the <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color> as viewed from Earth, many stars appear behind it. In
early May 2028, Centauri A will pass between the Earth and the distant red star 2MASS 14392160-6049528, when
there is a 45% probability that an Einstein ring will be observed. Other conjunctions will also occur in the coming
decades, allowing accurate measurement of proper motions and possibly giving information on planets.
Predicted future changes
Based on the system's common proper motion and radial velocities, Centauri will continue to change its position in the
sky significantly and will gradually brighten. For example, in about 6,200 <color=#3366CC>CE</color>, Centauri's true motion will cause an
extremely rare first-magnitude stellar conjunction with <color=#3366CC>Beta Centauri</color>, forming a brilliant optical <color=#3366CC>double star</color> in the
southern sky. It will then pass just north of the Southern Cross or <color=#3366CC>Crux</color>, before moving northwest and up towards the
present <color=#3366CC>celestial equator</color> and away from the <color=#3366CC>galactic plane</color>. By about 26,700 <color=#3366CC>CE</color>, in the present-day constellation of
<color=#3366CC>Hydra</color>, Centauri will reach perihelion at 0.90 pc away, though later calculations suggest that this will occur in 27,000
AD. At its closest approach, Centauri will attain a maximum <color=#3366CC>apparent magnitude</color> of 0.86, comparable to present-day
magnitude of <color=#3366CC>Canopus</color>, but it will not surpass that of <color=#3366CC>Sirius</color>, which will brighten incrementally over the next 60,000
years, and will continue to be the brightest star as seen from Earth (other than the Sun) for the next 210,000 years.
Stellar system
Alpha Centauri is a triple star system, with its two main stars, A and B, together comprising a <color=#3366CC>binary</color> component. The
AB designation, or older A×B, denotes the mass centre of a main binary system relative to companion star(s) in a
multiple star system. AB-C refers to the component of Proxima Centauri in relation to the central binary, being the
distance between the centre of mass and the outlying companion. Because the distance between Proxima (C) and
either of Alpha Centauri A or B is similar, the AB binary system is sometimes treated as a single gravitational object.
Orbital properties
The A and B components of Alpha Centauri have an orbital period of 79.762 years. Their orbit is moderately <color=#3366CC>eccentric</color>,
as it has an eccentricity of almost 0.52; their closest approach or <color=#3366CC>periastron</color> is 11.2 AU, or about the distance between
the Sun and Saturn; and their furthest separation or <color=#3366CC>apastron</color> is 35.6 AU, about the distance between the Sun and
Pluto. The most recent <color=#3366CC>periastron</color> was in August 1955 and the next will occur in May 2035; the most recent <color=#3366CC>apastron</color>
was in May 1995 and will next occur in 2075.
Viewed from Earth, the apparent orbit of A and B means that their separation and <color=#3366CC>position angle</color> (PA) are in continuous
change throughout their projected orbit. Observed stellar positions in 2019 are separated by 4.92 <color=#3366CC>arcsec</color> through the
PA of 337.1°, increasing to 5.49 arcsec through 345.3° in 2020. The closest recent approach was in February 2016, at
4.0 arcsec through the PA of 300°. The observed maximum separation of these stars is about 22 arcsec, while the
minimum distance is 1.7 arcsec. The widest separation occurred during February 1976, and the next will be in January
Alpha Centauri C is about 13000 AU from Alpha Centauri AB, equivalent to about 5% of the distance between Alpha
Centauri AB and the Sun. Until 2017, measurements of its small speed and its trajectory were of too little accuracy and
duration in years to determine whether it is bound to Alpha Centauri AB or unrelated.
Radial velocity measurements made in 2017 were precise enough to show that Proxima Centauri and Alpha Centauri
AB are gravitationally bound. The orbital period of Proxima Centauri is approximately 511000 years, with an eccentricity
of 0.5, much more eccentric than <color=#3366CC>Mercury</color>'s. Proxima Centauri comes within 4100 AU of AB at periastron, and its
apastron occurs at 12300 AU.
Physical properties
<color=#3366CC>Asteroseismic</color> studies, <color=#3366CC>chromospheric activity</color>, and stellar rotation (gyrochronology) are all consistent with the Alpha
Centauri system being similar in age to, or slightly older than, the Sun. Asteroseismic analyses that incorporate tight
observational constraints on the stellar parameters for the Alpha Centauri stars have yielded age estimates of 4.85 Gyr,
5.0 Gyr, 5.2 ± 1.9 Gyr, 6.4 Gyr, and 6.52 Gyr. Age estimates for the stars based on chromospheric activity (Calcium H
& K emission) yield 4.4 ± 2.1 Gyr, whereas gyrochronology yields 5.0 Gyr. <color=#3366CC>Stellar evolution</color> theory implies both stars
are slightly older than the Sun at 5 to 6 billion years, as derived by their mass and spectral characteristics.
From the <color=#3366CC>orbital elements</color>, the total mass of Alpha Centauri AB is about solar masses – or twice that of the Sun. The
average individual stellar masses are about solar masses and solar masses, respectively, though slightly different
masses have also been quoted in recent years, such as solar masses and solar masses, totaling solar masses. Alpha
Centauri A and B have <color=#3366CC>absolute magnitudes</color> of +4.38 and +5.71, respectively.
Alpha Centauri AB System
Alpha Centauri A
Alpha Centauri A, also known as Rigil Kentaurus, is the principal member, or primary, of the binary system. It is a
solar-like <color=#3366CC>main-sequence</color> star with a similar yellowish colour, whose <color=#3366CC>stellar classification</color> is <color=#3366CC>spectral type</color> G2-V; it is
about 10% more massive than the Sun, with a radius about 22% larger. When considered among the individual
brightest stars in the night sky, it is the fourth-brightest at an apparent magnitude of +0.01, being slightly fainter than
<color=#3366CC>Arcturus</color> at an <color=#3366CC>apparent magnitude</color> of 0.05.
The type of <color=#3366CC>magnetic activity</color> on Alpha Centauri A is comparable to that of the Sun, showing <color=#3366CC>coronal</color> variability due to
star spots, as modulated by the rotation of the star. However, since 2005 the activity level has fallen into a deep
minimum that might be similar to the Sun's historical Maunder Minimum. Alternatively, it may have a very long stellar
activity cycle and is slowly recovering from a minimum phase.
Alpha Centauri B
Alpha Centauri B, also known as Toliman, is the secondary star of the binary system. It is a main-sequence star of
spectral type K1-V, making it more an orange colour than Alpha Centauri A; it has around 90% of the mass of the Sun
and a 14% smaller diameter. Although it has a lower luminosity than A, Alpha Centauri B emits more energy in the
<color=#3366CC>X-ray</color> band. Its <color=#3366CC>light curve</color> varies on a short time scale, and there has been at least one observed <color=#3366CC>flare</color>. It is more
magnetically active than Alpha Centauri A, showing a cycle of 8.2 yr compared to 11 years for the Sun, and has about
half the minimum-to-peak variation in coronal luminosity of the Sun. This cycle was recently re-estimated based on
more than 20 years of high-resolution spectroscopic observations of the CaIIH&K lines showing a cycle of 7.8 yr. Alpha
Centauri B has an apparent magnitude of +1.35, slightly dimmer than <color=#3366CC>Mimosa</color>.
Alpha Centauri C
Alpha Centauri C, better known as Proxima Centauri, is a small main-sequence <color=#3366CC>red dwarf</color> of spectral class M6-Ve. It
has an <color=#3366CC>absolute magnitude</color> of +15.60, over 20,000 times fainter than the Sun. Its mass is calculated to be solar
masses. It is the closest star to the Sun but is too faint to be visible to the naked eye.
Planetary system
The Alpha Centauri system as a whole has two confirmed planets, both of them around Proxima Centauri. While other
planets have been claimed to exist around all of the stars, none of the discoveries have been confirmed.
Planets of Alpha Centauri A
In 2021, a candidate planet named Candidate 1 (or C1) was detected around Alpha Centauri A, thought to orbit at
approximately 1.1 AU with a period of about one year, and to have a mass between that of Neptune and one-half that
of Saturn, though it may be a dust disk or an artefact. The possibility of C1 being a background star has been ruled out.
If this candidate is confirmed, the temporary name C1 will most likely be replaced with the scientific designation Alpha
Centauri Ab in accordance with current naming conventions.
GO Cycle 1 observations are planned for the <color=#3366CC>James Webb Space Telescope</color> (JWST) to search for planets around
Alpha Centauri A, as well as observations of Epsilon Muscae. The coronographic observations, which occurred on July
26 and 27, 2023, were failures, though there are follow-up observations in March 2024. Pre-launch estimates predicted
that JWST will be able to find planets with a radius of 5 at 1–3 AU. Multiple observations every 3–6 months could push
the limit down to 3. Post-launch estimates based on observations of HIP 65426 b find that JWST will be able to find
planets even closer to Alpha Centauri A and could find a 5 planet at 0.5–2.5 AU. Candidate 1 has an estimated radius
between 3.3–11 and orbits at 1.1 AU.
Observations with the James Webb Space Telescope in August 2024 uncovered a point source which may be an
exoplanet at a separation of 2 astronomical units, believed to be the same object detected in 2021. This object is
confirmed not to be a background object, and is unlikely to be an instrumental artifact, potentially making it an
exoplanet. It was not recovered and needs additional observations to be confirmed as a planet; there is a 52% chance
it was not re-observed due to the orbital motion. If it is an exoplanet, it should have a mass between 90 and 150 <color=#3366CC>Earth</color>
<color=#3366CC>masses</color>, a radius between 1.0 and 1.1 and a temperature of 225 K.
Planets of Alpha Centauri B
The first claim of a planet around Alpha Centauri B was that of Alpha Centauri Bb in 2012, which was proposed to be
an Earth-mass planet in a 3.2-day orbit. This was refuted in 2015 when the apparent planet was shown to be an
artefact of the way the radial velocity data was processed.
A search for <color=#3366CC>transits</color> of planet Bb was conducted with the <color=#3366CC>Hubble Space Telescope</color> from 2013 to 2014. This search
detected one potential transit-like event, which could be associated with a different planet with a radius around. This
planet would most likely orbit Alpha Centauri B with an orbital period of 20.4 days or less, with only a 5% chance of it
having a longer orbit. The median of the likely orbits is 12.4 days. Its orbit would likely have an eccentricity of 0.24 or
less. It could have lakes of molten lava and would be far too close to Alpha Centauri B to harbour <color=#3366CC>life</color>. If confirmed, this
planet might be called Alpha Centauri Bc. However, the name has not been used in the literature, as it is not a claimed
discovery.
Planets of Proxima Centauri
<color=#3366CC>Proxima Centauri b</color> or Alpha Centauri Cb is a terrestrial planet discovered in 2016 by astronomers at the <color=#3366CC>European</color>
<color=#3366CC>Southern Observatory</color> (ESO). It has an estimated minimum mass of 1.17 (<color=#3366CC>Earth masses</color>) and orbits approximately
0.049 <color=#3366CC>AU</color> from Proxima Centauri, placing it in the star's <color=#3366CC>habitable zone</color>.
The discovery of Proxima Centauri c was formally published in 2020 and could be a <color=#3366CC>super-Earth</color> or mini-Neptune. It has
a mass of roughly 7 and orbits about 1.49 AU from Proxima Centauri with a period of 1928 days. In June 2020, a
possible direct imaging detection of the planet hinted at the presence of a large ring system. However, a 2022 study
disputed the existence of this planet. As of 2025, evidence for Proxima c remains inconclusive; observations with the
NIRPS spectrograph were unable to confirm it, but found hints of a lower-amplitude signal with a similar period.
A 2020 paper refining Proxima b's mass excludes the presence of extra companions with masses above at periods
shorter than 50 days, but the authors detected a radial-velocity curve with a periodicity of 5.15 days, suggesting the
presence of a planet with a mass of about. This planet, Proxima Centauri d, was detected in 2022 and later confirmed
Hypothetical planets
Additional planets may exist in the Alpha Centauri system, either orbiting Alpha Centauri A or Alpha Centauri B
individually, or in large orbits around Alpha Centauri AB. Because both stars are fairly similar to the Sun (in age and
<color=#3366CC>metallicity</color>, for example), astronomers have been especially interested in making detailed searches for planets in the
Alpha Centauri system. Several established planet-hunting teams have used various <color=#3366CC>radial velocity</color> or star <color=#3366CC>transit</color>
methods in their searches around these two bright stars.No observational studies have succeeded in finding evidence
for <color=#3366CC>brown dwarfs</color> or <color=#3366CC>gas giants</color>.
In 2009, computer simulations showed that a planet might have been able to form near the inner edge of Alpha
Centauri B's habitable zone, which extends from 0.5–0.9 AU from the star. Certain special assumptions, such as
considering that the Alpha Centauri pair may have initially formed with a wider separation and later moved closer to
each other (as might be possible if they formed in a dense <color=#3366CC>star cluster</color>), would permit an accretion-friendly environment
farther from the star. Bodies around Alpha Centauri A would be able to orbit at slightly farther distances due to its
stronger gravity. In addition, the lack of any brown dwarfs or gas giants in close orbits around Alpha Centauri make the
likelihood of terrestrial planets greater than otherwise. A theoretical study indicates that a radial velocity analysis might
detect a hypothetical planet of in Alpha Centauri B's <color=#3366CC>habitable zone</color>.
Radial velocity measurements of Alpha Centauri B made with the High Accuracy Radial Velocity Planet Searcher
<color=#3366CC>spectrograph</color> were sufficiently sensitive to detect a planet within the habitable zone of the star (i.e. with an orbital period
P = 200 days), but no planets were detected.
A 2016 estimate placed the probability of finding an Earth-like planet around Alpha Centauri at roughly 75%. The
observational thresholds for planet detection in the habitable zones by the radial velocity method are currently (2017)
estimated to be about for Alpha Centauri A, for Alpha Centauri B, and for <color=#3366CC>Proxima Centauri</color>.
Early computer-generated models of planetary formation predicted the existence of <color=#3366CC>terrestrial planets</color> around both
Alpha Centauri A and B, but most recent numerical investigations have shown that the gravitational pull of the
companion star renders the accretion of planets difficult. Despite these difficulties, given the similarities to the Sun in
<color=#3366CC>spectral types</color>, star type, age and probable stability of the orbits, it has been suggested that this stellar system could
hold one of the best possibilities for harbouring <color=#3366CC>extraterrestrial life</color> on a potential planet.

In the <color=#3366CC>Solar System</color>, it was once thought that <color=#3366CC>Jupiter</color> and <color=#3366CC>Saturn</color> were probably crucial in perturbing <color=#3366CC>comets</color> into the
inner Solar System, providing the inner planets with a source of water and various other ices. However, since isotope

measurements of the <color=#3366CC>deuterium</color> to <color=#3366CC>hydrogen</color> (D/H) ratio in comets <color=#3366CC>Halley</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hyakutake</color>, <color=#3366CC>Hale–Bopp</color>, 2002T7, and Tuttle
yield values approximately twice that of Earth's oceanic water, more recent models and research predict that less than
10% of Earth's water was supplied from comets. In the Centauri system, Proxima Centauri may have influenced the
planetary disk as the Centauri system was forming, enriching the area around Alpha Centauri with volatile materials.
This would be discounted if, for example, Centauri B happened to have <color=#3366CC>gas giants</color> orbiting Centauri A (or vice versa),
or if Centauri A and B themselves were able to perturb comets into each other's inner systems, as Jupiter and Saturn
presumably have done in the Solar System. Such icy bodies probably also reside in <color=#3366CC>Oort clouds</color> of other planetary
systems. When they are influenced gravitationally by either the gas giants or disruptions by passing nearby stars, many
of these icy bodies then travel star-wards. Such ideas also apply to the close approach of Alpha Centauri or other stars
to the Solar system, when, in the distant future, the <color=#3366CC>Oort Cloud</color> might be disrupted enough to increase the number of
active comets.
To be in the <color=#3366CC>habitable zone</color>, a planet around Alpha Centauri A would have an orbital radius of between about 1.2 and
2.1 AU so as to have similar planetary temperatures and conditions for liquid water to exist. For the slightly less
luminous and cooler Centauri B, the habitable zone is between about 0.7 and 1.2 AU.
With the goal of finding evidence of such planets, both Proxima Centauri and Centauri AB were among the listed
"Tier-1" target stars for <color=#3366CC>NASA</color>'s Space Interferometry Mission (S.I.M.). Detecting planets as small as three
Earth-masses or smaller within two AU of a "Tier-1" target would have been possible with this new instrument. The
S.I.M. mission, however, was cancelled due to financial issues in 2010.
Circumstellar discs
Based on observations between 2007 and 2012, a study found a slight excess of emissions in the 24 m
(mid/far-infrared) band surrounding Centauri AB, which may be interpreted as evidence for a sparse <color=#3366CC>circumstellar disc</color>
or dense <color=#3366CC>interplanetary dust</color>. The total mass was estimated to be between to the mass of the <color=#3366CC>Moon</color>, or 10–100 times
the mass of the Solar System's <color=#3366CC>zodiacal cloud</color>. If such a disc existed around both stars, Centauri A's disc would likely
be stable to 2.8 AU, and Centauri B's would likely be stable to 2.5 AU This would put A's disc entirely within the frost
line, and a small part of B's outer disc just outside.
View from this system
The sky from Centauri AB would appear much as it does from the Earth, except that <color=#3366CC>Centaurus</color>'s brightest star, being
Centauri AB itself, would be absent from the constellation. The Sun would appear as a white star of <color=#3366CC>apparent</color>
<color=#3366CC>magnitude</color> +0.5, roughly the same as the average brightness of <color=#3366CC>Betelgeuse</color> from Earth. It would be at the antipodal
point of Centauri AB's current <color=#3366CC>right ascension</color> and <color=#3366CC>declination</color>, at (2000), in eastern <color=#3366CC>Cassiopeia</color>, easily outshining all the
rest of the stars in the <color=#3366CC>constellation</color>. With the placement of the Sun east of the magnitude 3.4 star Epsilon Cassiopeiae,
nearly in front of the Heart Nebula, the "W" line of stars of Cassiopeia would have a "/W" shape.
Other nearby stars' placements may be affected somewhat drastically. <color=#3366CC>Sirius</color>, at 9.2 light years away from the system,
would still be the brightest star in the night sky, with a magnitude of -1.2, but would be located in <color=#3366CC>Orion</color> less than a
degree away from Betelgeuse. <color=#3366CC>Procyon</color>, which would also be at a slightly further distance than from the Sun, would
move to outshine <color=#3366CC>Pollux</color> in the middle of <color=#3366CC>Gemini</color>.
A planet around either Centauri A or B would see the other star as a very bright secondary. For example, an Earth-like
planet at 1.25 AU from Cen A (with a revolution period of 1.34 years) would get Sun-like illumination from its primary,
and Cen B would appear 5.7–8.6 magnitudes dimmer (21.0 to 18.2), 190–2,700 times dimmer than Cen A but still
150–2,100 times brighter than the full Moon. Conversely, an Earth-like planet at 0.71 AU from Cen B (with a revolution
period of 0.63 years) would get nearly Sun-like illumination from its primary, and Cen A would appear 4.6–7.3
magnitudes dimmer (22.1 to 19.4), 70 to 840 times dimmer than Cen B but still 470–5,700 times brighter than the full
Moon.
Proxima Centauri would appear dim as one of many stars, being magnitude 4.5 at its current distance, and magnitude
2.6 at periastron.
Future exploration
Alpha Centauri is a first target for crewed or robotic <color=#3366CC>interstellar exploration</color>. Using current spacecraft technologies,
crossing the distance between the Sun and Alpha Centauri would take several millennia, though the possibility of
nuclear pulse propulsion or laser light sail technology, as considered in the Breakthrough Starshot program, could
make the journey to Alpha Centauri in 20 years. An objective of such a mission would be to make a fly-by of, and
possibly photograph, planets that might exist in the system. The existence of <color=#3366CC>Proxima Centauri b</color>, announced by the
<color=#3366CC>European Southern Observatory</color> (ESO) in August 2016, would be a target for the Starshot program.
<color=#3366CC>NASA</color> released a mission concept in 2017 that would send a spacecraft to Alpha Centauri in 2069, scheduled to
coincide with the 100th anniversary of the first crewed lunar landing in 1969, <color=#3366CC>Apollo 11</color>. Even at 10% of the <color=#3366CC>speed of</color>
<color=#3366CC>light</color> (about 108 million km/h), which NASA experts say may be possible, it would take a spacecraft 44 years to reach
the system, by the year 2113, and would take another 4 years for a signal, by the year 2117 to reach Earth. The
concept received no further funding or development.
In culture
Alpha Centauri has been recognized and associated throughout history, particularly in the <color=#3366CC>Southern Hemisphere</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Polynesians</color> have been using Alpha Centauri for their <color=#3366CC>star navigation</color> and have called it Kamailehope. In the
Ngarrindjeri culture of Australia, Alpha Centauri represents with <color=#3366CC>Beta Centauri</color> two sharks chasing a <color=#3366CC>stingray</color>, the

<color=#3366CC>Southern Cross</color>, and in <color=#3366CC>Incan</color> culture it with Beta Centauri form the eyes of a <color=#3366CC>llama</color>-shaped <color=#3366CC>dark constellation</color>
embedded in the band of stars that the visible <color=#3366CC>Milky Way</color> forms in the sky. In ancient Egypt it was also revered and in
China it is known as part of the South Gate asterism.
The Sagan Planet Walk in Ithaca, New York, is a walkable scale model of the solar system. An obelisk representing the
scaled position of Alpha Centauri has been added at Imiloa Astronomy Center in Hawaii.
